translations.8aa4fc9253d029c0e342f1bd: The mission moves from the task down to the doubt criterion: it’s the why that turns an order into a decision.
translations.72b1d553d3f818ba2e916145: ⟪P0⟫Task⟪P1⟫the concrete action, with a verb and an object.
translations.e1c5555be536474a8d3628ab: ⟪P0⟫Why⟪P1⟫the real problem that the task solves.
translations.3174e67601f8965ccdd7b0d4: ✓ Write the why as a painful problem, with a number if you have one: “I lose 2 hours a day”.
translations.b084eb4e08308ef140127231: ✗ Use generic whys like “improve customer service,” which don’t help you decide anything.
translations.413edc1e8f27de73446bbd4c: Choose a task you want to delegate and write the mission in two lines: the task and the why.
translations.ff80da59d91880e5b362828d: Store example: “Reply to customers about order status. This matters because I lose 2 hours a day with the same question and the customer keeps waiting.” The why shows the response has to be fast and correct, not just a nice-sounding text.
translations.528f4ba4f8b79424834a5bda: The tree shows how a large order is broken down until it reaches a small enough task to delegate and verify.
translations.b7f3aab024d7e7798b97ade5: ⟪P0⟫Employment⟪P1⟫the big whole set, like serving customers.
translations.f095e7759d8d9791253f00ce: ⟪P0⟫Process⟪P1⟫a part with a beginning and an end, like after-sales.
translations.3e8405815907512c9276c85c: ⟪P0⟫Task⟪P1⟫a repeatable action, like updating order status.
translations.bc6f68297bc8555c91084fb6: ⟪P0⟫Delivery⟪P1⟫what comes out at the end, like the sent response.
translations.0afcd4e07875a24ad34f4e57: Take care of the business: identify the initial condition.
translations.74d5b9d13a359c446fbf7123: Customer service: apply the described decision.
translations.59ea41155b6e904156e71bc8: Order status: check the effect in the example.
translations.68d8f24a446727150e0ba488: Response sent: record the output evidence.
translations.b46ad1b328615158292dd66e: ✓ Start with the most repeated, lowest-risk task, and only then create the second agent.
translations.f8535fd93243e746beef4fc5: ✗ Set up an “all-purpose agent” with a giant instruction that nobody can test.
translations.dc5da8ec612965f47328b6a9: Take one area of your work and split it into three delegable tasks and one that stays with you.
translations.f47aa02362c2c647e82ace7c: Accountant office example: check documents received; list what’s missing by customer; set up the reminder for pending items. Stays with you: talk to the customer about the fine. The one that stays is always the one with the highest risk or the one that requires judgment.
translations.bf1207632a219f7868a42a32: The cycle shows that the tiebreak rule is born from a conflict, is applied, generates a log entry, and is adjusted by real cases.
translations.7fb0280d0abe91fbe6876ad5: ⟪P0⟫Conflict⟪P1⟫two good things that can’t fit together.
translations.281e75a3c1c4246245d600da: ⟪P0⟫Winner⟪P1⟫the priority that wins, written out in full.
translations.23ba4fb1d30fe0d3216b3b95: ⟪P0⟫Action in uncertainty⟪P1⟫what to do when no rule resolves it.
translations.993293f0ee57ef6ecb464a04: ⟪P0⟫Review⟪P1⟫adjust the rule when a real case shows it failed.
translations.19d7132615c38e0084d564dd: ✓ Write the tiebreaker using a concrete example from your business right below it.
translations.b4bf548df01c1aefe08ac179: ✗ List ten priorities that are “all important” without saying which one wins.
translations.c6f78988c757170bf512bd07: Write a tiebreak rule for your agent in the format “X comes before Y” and provide an example.
translations.40097d6cd46ffe908bb410c0: Professor example: “Fairness to the student comes before finishing fast: if the writing is illegible or off-topic, mark review and don’t give a grade.” Notice that the rule says what to do, not only what to value.
translations.bb760bae682ab6d3ba7c6bc0: Context: what you’d explain on the first day
translations.8b4a026413c98694cb21d3d3: The layers show what the agent needs to hear on the first day, from the most general to the most specific.
